whyThis.en: The rolled omelette is the last step in eggs. It asks for gentle heat and a quick hand.

concept.en: Eggs set fast and keep cooking after they leave the heat. Stir early for small soft curds, stop while the top still looks wet, and roll before it firms up.

text.en: Crack the eggs into a bowl. Add the salt and pepper.
Whisk until no streaks of white are left.

tip.en: Stop there. Too much air makes an omelette spongy.

text.en: Melt half the butter in a pan over medium heat. Stir the spinach until it wilts, then tip it onto a plate.
Melt the rest of the butter in the same pan. Pour in the eggs and stir in small circles until you see soft, wet curds.

tip.en: Small curds now make a tender omelette later.

text.en: Stop stirring and let the bottom set. Scatter the spinach and the grated cheese down the middle.

tip.en: The top should still look a little wet. It keeps cooking as you roll.

text.en: Tilt the pan and roll the omelette over itself, from the handle side to the far edge.

tip.en: Pale and smooth is the goal. Brown means the pan was too hot.

text.en: Roll it out onto a plate, seam side down.

question.en: Why stop stirring while the eggs still look wet?

answers.en: Because eggs keep cooking from their own heat
So the butter does not burn

explanation.en: Eggs carry on setting after you stop. Pull back early and the middle stays soft.
